newsitem.title: USA: Food Lion ask for "very large" damages.
newsitem.headline: Food Lion ask for "very large" damages.

text.p: An attorney for Food Lion suggested Monday a federal jury order "very large" punitive damages against the ABC television network for its 1992 hidden camera report alleging the grocer engaged in unsanitary food handling practices.
In his closing arguments, attorney Timothy Barber repeatedly told the jury that the only way to stop other hidden camera investigations that break the law was to award financial damages.
"Punitive damages is the way to tell them so they can hear you," Barber said.
Barber did not specify to jurors an amount for punitive damages. Media reports indicated that Food Lion would seek up to $2 billion, but the company would not confirm the figure.
Barber told the jury that ABC had 1995 profits of $1.31 billion and asked the panel to consider that when determining damages.

Salisbury, N.C.-based grocer Food Lion sued ABC, a New York-based unit of Walt Disney Co., over a PrimeTime Live hidden camera report that ran in November 1992, alleging Food Lion repackaged spoiled meat and fish and sold outdated merchandise.
Barber suggested the jury order senior producer Ira Rosen and PrimeTime Live executive producer Richard Kaplan to pay a minimum of $50,000 each in damages.
As for two producers who worked undercover at Food Lion stores, he did not specify damages but suggested jurors take their salaries into account.
"Reporters all over the country need to know when you cross the line, you're going to be punished," Barber said.
Food Lion last month was awarded compensatory damages of $1,400 after the jury found ABC and its producers committed fraud, trespass and breach of loyalty.
The producers worked in two Food Lion stores in the Carolinas with cameras hidden in their hair and audio recorders under their smocks.
U.S. District Judge Carlton Tilley will instruct the jury Tuesday morning, before the panel begins deliberations.
